Variants.Content: Corn City is a farming stronghold in the West. The Westerlands are famous for their gold, but gold cannot fill an army; the river valleys, fields, mills and granaries are also the base of Lannister power. The name of Corn City refers directly to its function: the harvest determines taxes, livestock wintering, and how many people the lord can provide in times of crisis. Such inland castles are often far away from the naval battles and jousts in poetry, but life best shows the cost of war-grain requisitions, trampled fields, farmers who have lost their labor, and springs that cannot be planted on time.

Entry Cornfield Local families also relied on mining tunnels, pastures, mountain roads, gold and silver circulation and the market sheltered by Casterly Rock; if any road, well or dock failed, the price would fall first on them.

Entry Cornfield They also recognize the accents, laws, and credentials of the West; reputations can travel great distances from taverns, but true distances must still be measured by wheel, oar, or horse's hooves.

Entry Cornfield If you can supply supplies, avoid danger, and find a guide, it is worth marking in your itinerary; if you don't have these three things, no matter how loud your family name is, it won't be able to save the lost.

The traces left by generations of people in Maize City are half hidden in the stone walls, wooden beams, iron doors, tombs, and the seams left by generations of repairs, and the other half are hidden in the stone carvings left by the seven gods, family tombs, and the authority of the lords. A stronghold was therefore not just a lord's hall, but also a place where weddings and funerals, vows, labor and local memories recurred.

Entry Cornfield They care about the mines, pastures, mountain roads, the circulation of gold and silver, and the market under the protection of Casterly Rock. They also look at whether seeds are left after the grain collection and whether the city gates are open in times of disaster. When people from afar see the coat of arms, what they see is whether there will be food to eat tomorrow.
